title: Narrator's point of view
subject: READING
subtopic: Analyze Point of View, Features, and Structure

slides.title: The narrator has a view
slides.text:
The **narrator** tells the story.

The narrator has a **view**: what they think and feel about things in the story.

slides.title: Like or not like?
slides.text:
Some narrators **like** something. They use words like **love, fun, best**.

Some narrators **do not like** something. They use words like **hate, boring, worst**.

slides.title: How to find it
slides.text:
1. Find what the narrator talks about.
2. Look for **feeling words**.
3. Ask: **Does the narrator like it or not?**

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
Find the narrator's **feeling words**.

Tap the sentences that show what the narrator **thinks** or **feels**.

Those sentences prove the narrator's view.

sentences.t: I go to the zoo with my class.
The lions are the best part.
I love to watch them sleep in the sun.

example.explain:
The narrator says the lions are **the best part** and **I love** to watch them.

The narrator **likes** the lions.

together.passage: Rainy days are the best days. I jump in the puddles. Mom says to come inside. Splashing is so much fun!
together.stem: What does the narrator think about rainy days?
options: The narrator loves them.
The narrator hates them.
The narrator is scared of them.
The narrator does not see them.
together.hint: Look for feeling words. Does the narrator say rain is fun?
together.good: Yes! The narrator says rainy days are the best and fun. The narrator loves them.

sentences: Rainy days are the best days.
evidence.stem: The answer was: the narrator loves rainy days. Tap 2 sentences that show the narrator's feelings.
evidence.wrong: This sentence tells what someone does. Find the sentences with feeling words like best or fun.

checks.passage: I have to clean my room. It takes so long. Cleaning is the most boring job in the world.
checks.stem: What does the narrator think about cleaning?
options: It is fun.
It is fast.
It is easy.
It is boring.
checks.why: The narrator says cleaning is the most boring job in the world.

checks.passage: My grandma makes the best rice. It is soft and warm. I always ask for more.
checks.stem: Which sentence shows that the narrator loves Grandma's rice?
options: It is soft.
My grandma makes the best rice.
Grandma cooks.
It is warm.
checks.why: The narrator says it is the best rice. The word best shows the narrator's view.

checks.passage: Our new teacher is very kind. She smiles every day. She helps me when I am stuck.
checks.stem: How does the narrator feel about the new teacher?
options: Scared of her
Angry with her
Likes her
Does not know her
checks.why: The narrator says the teacher is kind, smiles and helps. The narrator likes her.

again.title: Happy words, unhappy words
again.text:
Circle the **happy words**: love, best, fun, great.

Circle the **unhappy words**: hate, boring, bad, worst.

Which kind does the narrator use more?
again.example:
"I think football is great. It is the best game ever."

Happy words: **great**, **best**. The narrator likes football.

slides.title: The narrator's attitude
slides.text:
A narrator's **attitude** is how they feel about the events or characters: proud, worried, amused, annoyed.

The attitude shows in the narrator's **word choice**.

slides.title: Viewpoint shapes the story
slides.text:
The narrator's view **affects** what we read.

A narrator who loves the beach will describe its warm sand and blue water. A narrator who hates it will describe the burning sun and sand in their shoes.

slides.title: Find the clues
slides.text:
1. What does the narrator **describe**?
2. Which words are **positive** or **negative**?
3. What do those words show about the narrator's attitude?

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
To prove the narrator's attitude:

1. Find **describing words** the narrator chooses.
2. Find what the narrator **thinks** or **wishes**.
3. Choose the attitude **most** of these words show.

Tap the sentences with the strongest clue words.

sentences.t: My little brother Faisal is a whirlwind.
He knocks over my towers, colours on my homework and eats my snacks.
Still, when he falls asleep on my shoulder, I would not trade him for anything.

example.explain:
At first, the narrator sounds **annoyed**: a whirlwind who wrecks things.

But the last sentence shows deep **love**. The narrator's attitude: annoyed but loving.

together.passage: For years, the empty lot at the end of our street was full of rubbish and dust. This spring, the city turned it into a park. It is truly wonderful: green grass, shady trees and a path where my grandfather walks every evening. Now the street is full of laughter instead of silence. In my opinion, it is the perfect gift for our neighbourhood.
together.stem: What is the narrator's attitude toward the new park?
options: Bored, because the park has nothing new
Worried, because the park is not safe
Angry, because the old field is gone
Delighted, because the park has changed the neighbourhood
together.hint: Look at the describing words the narrator uses for the park and the people in it.
together.good: Yes! Words like wonderful, laughter and perfect show the narrator is delighted.

sentences: For years, the empty lot at the end of our street was full of rubbish and dust.
This spring, the city turned it into a park.
It is truly wonderful: green grass, shady trees and a path where my grandfather walks every evening.
Now the street is full of laughter instead of silence.
In my opinion, it is the perfect gift for our neighbourhood.
evidence.stem: The answer was: the narrator is delighted. Tap 2 sentences that show the narrator's attitude.
evidence.wrong: This sentence gives facts about what the lot was or when it changed. Find the narrator's describing and opinion words.

checks.passage: We had to wait three hours at the airport. The seats were hard, the coffee was cold, and the screen kept saying "delayed". I will never fly on a holiday weekend again.
options: Excited
Calm
Frustrated
Proud
checks.why: Hard seats, cold coffee and "I will never fly ... again" all show frustration.

checks.passage: My sister Jana won the science prize. I watched her walk onto the stage, and I clapped until my hands hurt. She worked on that project every night for months, and she deserved every bit of it.
checks.stem: Which detail best shows the narrator's pride in Jana?
options: I clapped until my hands hurt.
My sister Jana won a prize.
She walked onto the stage.
The project was about science.
checks.why: Clapping until it hurts shows strong pride. The other details are facts that anyone could report.

checks.passage: Text A: I think the old souq is magical, with its narrow lanes and spice smells. Text B: I think the old souq is a maze, with lanes so narrow you can barely move.
checks.stem: How do the narrators' points of view affect the descriptions?
options: Both narrators describe the souq the same way.
Each narrator's attitude makes the same lanes seem good or bad.
Neither narrator has an opinion.
Text B describes a different market.
checks.why: Both see narrow lanes, but Text A calls the souq magical and Text B calls it a maze.

again.title: Thumbs and words
again.text:
Read the narrator's words. For each describing word, give it a **thumb up** (positive) or **thumb down** (negative).

More thumbs up = positive attitude. More thumbs down = negative attitude.
again.example:
"Our trip was exhausting, crowded and much too long."

exhausting: down. crowded: down. too long: down.

Attitude: **unhappy** about the trip.

slides.title: How authors build a viewpoint
slides.text:
Authors use **techniques** to show a narrator's point of view:

1. **Word choice:** positive or negative words
2. **Selection:** what the narrator chooses to describe or leave out
3. **Inner thoughts:** what the narrator thinks or wonders

slides.title: Effect on the reader
slides.text:
Because we see the story through the narrator's eyes, we often **share** their feelings.

If the narrator distrusts a character, we may distrust them too, even before we know the facts.

slides.title: Narrator vs. author
slides.text:
The narrator's view is not always the **author's** view.

An author may create a narrator with a strong opinion to make readers **think** about it.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
To identify a technique:

1. Find words or details that show the narrator's view.
2. Ask: **how** does the author show it? Word choice? Inner thoughts? What the narrator notices?
3. Explain the **effect** on what the reader thinks or feels.

sentences.t: The new boy strolled into class ten minutes late, as if the whole school belonged to him.
He dropped his bag with a thud and didn't even glance at the teacher.
I decided right then that we would never be friends.

example.explain:
The author uses **word choice** ("strolled", "as if the whole school belonged to him") to show the narrator's **negative** view.

Effect: the reader also starts to dislike the boy, though we do not yet know why he was late.

together.passage: My grandmother's house is small and old, with a blue door that sticks in summer. But stepping inside feels like wrapping myself in a warm blanket. The air always smells of cardamom and freshly baked bread. Her soft voice drifts from the kitchen, telling stories I have heard a hundred times and still love. There is no place on earth that feels more like home.
together.stem: Which technique does the author mainly use to show the narrator's point of view about her grandmother's house?
options: Facts and numbers about the house
Dialogue between the grandmother and a neighbour
Warm, sensory word choices that show the narrator's love
Describing the house from the grandmother's point of view
together.hint: Look at the describing words. Are they facts, or words that show the narrator's feelings?
together.good: Yes! Words like warm, comforting and soft, and memories of cardamom and stories, show the narrator's love.

sentences: My grandmother's house is small and old, with a blue door that sticks in summer.
But stepping inside feels like wrapping myself in a warm blanket.
The air always smells of cardamom and freshly baked bread.
Her soft voice drifts from the kitchen, telling stories I have heard a hundred times and still love.
There is no place on earth that feels more like home.
evidence.stem: The answer was: warm, sensory word choices that show love. Tap 2 sentences with these words.
evidence.wrong: This sentence gives plain facts about the house. Find sentences where the narrator's warm feelings come through.

checks.passage: I watched Coach Badr pace the sideline. He didn't shout like other coaches. He knelt beside each player during breaks and spoke quietly. I wondered why I had ever thought he was too soft. Our team had not lost a match all season.
checks.stem: How does the narrator's attitude toward the coach change?
options: From admiration to anger
From doubt to respect
From fear to boredom
It does not change.
checks.why: The narrator once thought he was too soft, but now sees his quiet method works. Doubt has become respect.

checks.passage: Everyone said the old fisherman was strange and unfriendly. I believed them, so I never spoke to him. It was only when he pulled my brother out of the sea that I learned his name.
checks.stem: What is the effect of telling this story from the narrator's point of view?
options: The reader learns the fisherman's thoughts from the start.
The reader knows the fisherman was kind all along.
The narrator explains the fisherman's whole life.
The reader shares the narrator's wrong idea until the rescue.
checks.why: We only know what the narrator believes, so we also think the fisherman is unfriendly until he saves the brother.

checks.passage: Our class trip to the museum was, I admit, better than I expected. I had planned to be bored. Instead, I spent an hour at the ancient coins and forgot to complain even once.
checks.stem: Which technique shows the narrator's changing view?
options: Comparing what the narrator expected with what happened
Describing the museum's history
Telling the story from the teacher's point of view
Using dialogue between two students
checks.why: The narrator says they planned to be bored, then describes forgetting to complain. The contrast shows a changing view.

again.title: Swap the narrator
again.text:
To see the narrator's effect, imagine **another** narrator telling the same events.

What would change? The difference shows what the first narrator's view adds.
again.example:
Narrator 1 (a cat-lover): "The kitten curled up on my lap, purring softly."
Narrator 2 (who is allergic): "The kitten climbed onto my lap, and my eyes began to itch."

Same event, **different views**.

slides.title: Can we trust the narrator?
slides.text:
Some narrators are **unreliable**: their view is limited, biased or mistaken.

They may misunderstand other characters, leave out facts, or describe themselves too kindly.

slides.title: Irony and the gap
slides.text:
When the reader understands **more** than the narrator, there is a gap. This gap creates **irony**.

Authors use it to make readers question the narrator and think more deeply.

slides.title: Techniques to notice
slides.text:
1. **Contradictions** between what the narrator says and what happens
2. **Other characters' reactions** that do not match the narrator's view
3. **Emotional language** that shows bias
4. **Missing information** the narrator does not mention

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
To analyse a narrator's viewpoint:

1. Note the narrator's claims and attitude.
2. Find evidence **inside the text** that supports or **contradicts** those claims.
3. Explain the effect: what does the reader understand that the narrator does not?

sentences.t: I am, without question, the best player on our team.
That is why I took every shot in yesterday's match, even when Omar was standing alone in front of the goal.
We lost four goals to nil, but that was clearly the goalkeeper's fault.
Strangely, nobody passed to me in the second half.

example.explain:
The narrator claims to be the best, but the details show he **ignored a free teammate** and **blames others**.

The reader sees what he does not: his teammates stopped passing because he was selfish. He is an **unreliable narrator**.

together.passage: Everyone knows I am the natural leader of our group, so naturally I made all the decisions for our history project. I chose the topic, the colours and the title, and I told the others exactly what to write. When Rana suggested adding a map, I explained kindly why it was a poor idea. For some reason, Rana and Dana exchanged a look and went quiet for the rest of the afternoon. The next day, they asked the teacher if they could join another group.
together.stem: How does the author show that the narrator's view of herself may not be accurate?
options: She admits openly that she was wrong about everything.
Her classmates' reactions do not match her description of herself.
She gives exact facts and numbers about her project.
The story is told by a narrator outside the story.
together.hint: Compare what the narrator says about herself with how the other girls act.
together.good: Yes! She says she is a great leader, but her friends exchange looks and quietly leave. Their reactions suggest a different picture.

sentences: Everyone knows I am the natural leader of our group, so naturally I made all the decisions for our history project.
I chose the topic, the colours and the title, and I told the others exactly what to write.
When Rana suggested adding a map, I explained kindly why it was a poor idea.
For some reason, Rana and Dana exchanged a look and went quiet for the rest of the afternoon.
The next day, they asked the teacher if they could join another group.
evidence.stem: The answer was: the classmates' reactions do not match her view. Tap the 2 sentences that show their reactions.
evidence.wrong: This sentence shows the narrator's own claims or actions. Find how the OTHER girls react.

checks.passage: My uncle says I am too young to understand business, but I know a great deal. Yesterday I sold my bicycle to a boy at school for half of what it cost. He was very grateful, and he said he had never met such a generous trader. I expect my uncle will be impressed.
checks.stem: What does the reader understand that the narrator does not?
options: The narrator made a poor deal, and the uncle may be right.
The narrator is an expert trader.
The uncle will be very impressed.
The boy paid too much for the bicycle.
checks.why: Selling for half price is a bad deal, and the boy's "generous" comment confirms it. The narrator misses this.

checks.passage: The narrator describes her new neighbour only as "the noisy woman next door" who "bangs things all day". Later, the narrator mentions in passing that the neighbour has been building a wheelchair ramp for her elderly father.
checks.stem: What is the effect of the narrator's word choice?
options: It makes the neighbour seem kind and gentle.
It shows the narrator understands the neighbour well.
It makes the reader judge the neighbour unfairly at first.
It explains how to build a ramp.
checks.why: Calling her "the noisy woman" leads us to dislike her, until we learn the noise comes from a kind act.

checks.passage: Two friends tell the story of the same football match. Khalid writes: "The referee was clearly against us from the first minute." Ziyad writes: "We made too many mistakes, and the other team deserved to win."
checks.stem: How does comparing the two narrators help the reader?
options: It proves that the referee was unfair.
It shows that both narrators agree completely.
It shows that Khalid is the more reliable narrator.
It shows that Khalid's view may be biased.
checks.why: Ziyad, from the same team, blames their mistakes. This suggests Khalid's view may be biased.

again.title: Claim vs. clue
again.text:
Make two lists:

**What the narrator claims** | **What the clues show**

If the lists do not match, the narrator may be unreliable.
again.example:
Claim: "Everyone loves my singing."
Clue: "My brother puts on his headphones whenever I start."

The lists do not match. The narrator may not be telling the whole truth.
